headline_en: Jobs after studying abroad: how to spot fake recruitment and visa sponsorship traps
summary_en: An education-section explainer warns international students looking for jobs after finishing studies abroad about fake job ads, fraudulent recruiters and paid 'guaranteed' visa sponsorship offers. It gives checks: verify the post on the company's own careers page, treat requests for money as a red flag, verify the recruiter's link to the company, and do not hand over passport, bank or immigration documents before verifying.

facts.statement: Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026), citing education-sector people: a job ad seen on LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp is not by itself proof that the job is real; international students who finish studies abroad should check whether the same post appears on the company's own website and careers page, and whether the duties and application process match.
facts.source_in_article: education-related people quoted by the article

facts.statement: Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): a demand for money in exchange for a job or visa sponsorship abroad is a major warning sign; in a normal recruitment process the company, not the job seeker, pays the recruiter.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): if a fee is requested in a job process abroad, the student should verify why it is charged, to whom it is paid and whether it is necessary; if in doubt, consult the university's career service or the international student support team.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): fraudsters targeting international graduates promise '100 percent guaranteed visa', 'guaranteed sponsorship' or 'guaranteed work visa' for money; the article says visa sponsorship actually depends on the employer, job type, candidate's qualifications and the country's immigration policy, so paid guaranteed-sponsorship promises are risky to trust without checking.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): when someone contacts a student claiming to represent an established company, check whether they really have a link to that company; using a Gmail or Outlook address is not proof of fraud by itself, but match the company website, official email domain, LinkedIn presence and contact details.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): genuine employers usually have steps such as application, interview, assessment or discussion with HR; an offer of a job within one or two days without detailed discussion or assessment is a warning sign.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): do not give a copy of your passport, bank account details or immigration documents before verifying the employer's identity and the company's legitimacy; extra checks are needed when there is pressure to decide quickly, a request for advance money, a guaranteed-sponsorship promise, or an offer that comes only through personal contact.

headline_en: Five teens and young men abducted on pretext of an outing, held and tortured by traffickers (Teknaf)
summary_en: Five teenagers and young men from Mithachhari, Ramu, Cox's Bazar were lured on 11 September 2026 with a promised trip to Teknaf's Marine Drive, then blindfolded, held, beaten and ransomed by a human trafficking gang that planned to send them by sea to Indonesia and Malaysia. SRB-15 rescued them on 20 September 2026 at Khonkarpara ghat near Sabrang Zero Point, Teknaf, and arrested Md. Anas alias Munna (21); a case was filed at Teknaf Model Police Station.

facts.statement: On the afternoon of 11 Sep 2026, members of a human trafficking gang picked up five teens and young men from Mithachhari area, Ramu upazila (Cox's Bazar) in a CNG auto-rickshaw, saying they would tour Teknaf's Marine Drive and beach; at night in Teknaf they were taken elsewhere on the pretext of staying at Md. Anas alias Munna's house, then blindfolded with a gamchha and taken to an unknown place.
facts.source_in_article: SRB-15 Assistant Director (Law and Media) A M Faruk

facts.statement: Prothom Alo (21 Sep 2026): the traffickers who abducted five youths from Ramu were trying to send them by sea from Teknaf to Indonesia and Malaysia, while collecting ransom from their families in instalments.
The five abducted youths (two aged 16, two aged 18, one aged 20) alleged they were held and physically tortured by the traffickers after abduction, and that ransom was demanded from their families.

At dawn on 20 Sep 2026 (Sunday), Special Response Battalion-15 (SRB) raided Khonkarpara ghat area next to Marine Drive at Sabrang Zero Point, Teknaf, rescued the five unharmed after 10 days, gave first aid, and arrested Md. Anas alias Munna (21); other gang members fled. Anas and the five victims were handed to Teknaf Model Police Station and a case was filed.
facts.source_in_article: SRB-15 Assistant Director A M Faruk

facts.statement: The victims' families submitted a written complaint to the SRB-15 Cox's Bazar office on 16 Sep 2026; SRB then used information technology to locate the gang members and carry out the raid.

headline_en: Full support for expatriates' initiatives is essential for the country (opinion)
summary_en: An opinion piece by Prof. Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed, convener of the Remittance Fair and president of the Bangladesh USA Chamber of Commerce and Industries, describes four years of trade and remittance fairs in New York with the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce. He says banks at the fair urged expatriates to send money through banks and authorised money transfer firms instead of hundi, and argues that rules of the NGO Affairs Bureau and Bangladesh Bank block expatriates from sending charitable donations to unregistered institutions in Bangladesh.

facts.statement: At the New York Remittance Fair, several large Bangladeshi banks held seminars asking expatriates to send money through banks and authorised money transfer institutions instead of hundi, and presented their special services, incentives and transfer security; some institutions held road shows in parts of New York on sending remittance through legal channels.
facts.source_in_article: Prof. Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed, convener, Remittance Fair (opinion)

facts.statement: The writer says remittance inflow from the United States to Bangladesh has grown significantly in recent years and that at times more foreign currency came from the United States than from some Middle Eastern countries (no figures given).

According to the writer, sending money from abroad to an institution in Bangladesh for charitable work is very difficult: the receiving institution is told to register as an NGO with the NGO Affairs Bureau, and that registration is hard to get because of delays and approval complexity; he names the NGO Affairs Bureau, the national security agency and Bangladesh Bank as sources of complexity.

The writer says a New York pharmacist friend, Liakat, wanted to donate USD 50,000 to the Sylhet kidney hospital (Kidney Foundation) during COVID, but it could not be sent because the foundation was not registered with the NGO Affairs Bureau; after about eight years as a charity hospital it still had not obtained registration, so donations from abroad cannot go directly to the hospital's bank account for free dialysis.

The writer urges the Bangladesh Bank governor and finance authorities not to limit expatriates' foreign currency transfers to individuals or NGO Affairs Bureau-registered bodies, and to let social organisations registered with the Ministry of Social Welfare, schools, colleges, universities, hospitals, cultural and environmental bodies and charities receive foreign donations legally under audit and reporting obligations.

The writer says this year's trade and remittance fair by the Bangladesh USA Chamber of Commerce and Industries with the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce was to be held on 17 Sep 2026 in New York City, with the New York governor expected as chief guest and senior US Small Business Administration (SBA) representatives attending.

The 2025 New York Remittance Fair's chief guest was Kelly Loeffler, head of the Small Business Administration under the Trump administration; leaders of Bangladeshi NRB business chambers from the UK, Italy, Poland and Canada attended for the first time.
The writer proposes that every expatriate Bangladeshi give at least USD 200 a year to education, health, agriculture, humanitarian aid, road repair or other public-welfare work in Bangladesh.

Under the SICIP-Barind University programme, 1,200 trainees in total will be trained between October 2026 and July 2028: 450 at the Rajshahi centre and 750 at the Dhaka centre.

The SICIP programme is taking steps to help trainees enter domestic and international job markets and to collaborate with employers and recruiting agencies, with the aim of new employment opportunities in Japan and other international labour markets.
SICIP's executive programme director is Mohammad Walid Hossain, Additional Secretary of the Finance Ministry; Barind University's vice-chancellor is Prof. Md. Khademul Islam Molla.

headline_en: From ration to farmer cards: why one ID now, and what it will contain
summary_en: A Prothom Alo explainer traces Bangladesh's card-based welfare schemes and the government's proposed 'One-ID' unified digital identity under the D-STAR project (2026 to 2031). In passing it reports that the 'Probashi card' for expatriates, a BNP election pledge announced by the expatriates' welfare minister in February 2026 as coming soon, has not yet been launched and is still in preparation.

facts.statement: A 'Probashi card' (প্রবাসী কার্ড) for expatriate Bangladeshis was a BNP election pledge; in February 2026 the expatriates' welfare minister announced it would be launched soon, but as of 5 Sep 2026 it had not been launched and was still in the preparation stage.

The ICT Division has proposed the 'Digital Service Transformation for Access and Resilience' (D-STAR) project, implemented by Bangladesh Computer Council, for 2026 to 2031, to give each citizen a permanent digital identity ('One-ID') from birth for health, education and other services; proposed cost BDT 9,193 crore, 20 crore cards to be produced for 18 crore citizens; sent to the Planning Commission for approval; contents of the card not yet decided.

Under the One-ID plan, existing cards such as the NID, Family Card and Farmer Card would gradually lose separate functions; the plan is still at an early stage, with the slogan 'One Citizen, One Digital ID, One Wallet'.

headline_en: Higher study abroad: how our young people fall into the push-pull trap (opinion)
summary_en: An opinion piece by Habib Rahman, a doctoral researcher at Curtin University, Australia, describes how international students, including many Bangladeshis across Australian cities, must work multiple jobs (restaurants, cleaning, delivery) to cover high tuition and living costs, so study becomes secondary. He says host countries tighten policies (higher fees, stricter English rules, age and study-gap limits, large proof of funds, rising refusals) when conditions change, and that some unscrupulous Bangladeshi agencies arrange fake bank statements and English certificates and make unrealistic job promises, leaving students with losses of several lakh taka when visas are refused.

facts.statement: The writer says a Sri Lankan student he knew in Perth, Australia, doing a two-year master's, would spend about 1 crore taka in Bangladeshi currency on the degree; the student worked from morning to night in a restaurant and a cleaning company and also delivered food on Uber, and was dismissed by his manager after breaking his hand at work and missing a few days.
facts.source_in_article: Habib Rahman, doctoral researcher, Curtin University (opinion)

facts.statement: The writer says in almost every Australian city a large share of Bangladeshi students have to support themselves through hard labour alongside study, working in restaurants, cleaning companies, ride-sharing or delivery, so that for many the struggle to survive makes study secondary.

The writer says when economic or political conditions change, destination countries in Europe, North America and Australia raise tuition fees, tighten English-language requirements, impose new limits on age and study gaps, demand proof of large financial means, restrict choice of subject, and visa risks rise for citizens of developing or politically unstable countries; visa refusal rates are rising.

The writer says some unscrupulous Bangladeshi agencies exploit students' wish to study abroad with promises of university admission, jobs, visas and an easy life abroad, sometimes preparing fake or staged bank statements, procuring English proficiency certificates, or making unrealistic promises of jobs abroad.

The writer says when a student visa is refused, a student can lose up to several lakh taka in application fees, university fees, agency charges, medical tests, documents, English tests and other costs.

The writer says students with full scholarships or strong finances have an easier time abroad, while others face uncertainty over whether they will keep a visa after study, find a job or be able to settle, amid anti-immigration politics and xenophobia.

headline_en: 68 data leaks in three years, no accountability or punishment
summary_en: A TechGlobal Institute (TGI) report records at least 68 data breaches in Bangladesh from January 2023 to May 2026 (36 government, 32 private), mostly detected by outsiders. It includes incidents tied to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's database, where passports, NIDs, e-TINs and financial and banking documents were at risk of exposure together, and three attempted intrusions in about six weeks in April and May 2026 into a migrant workers' database holding data on more than 1 million migrant workers.

facts.statement: TechGlobal Institute (TGI) report 'Breached and Unanswered: Bangladesh's Data Breach Epidemic (2023-2026)' says there were three attempted intrusions within about six weeks in April and May 2026 into the database of migrant workers (প্রবাসী শ্রমিকদের তথ্যভান্ডার), which holds data on more than 10 lakh (1 million) migrant workers.

TGI claims that in an incident linked to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's database, there was a risk that migrants' passports, NIDs, e-TINs and financial and banking documents could be exposed together.

TGI recorded at least 68 data breaches in Bangladesh from January 2023 to May 2026: 36 at government and 32 at private bodies; 7 in 2023, 27 in 2024, 14 in 2025 and 20 in January-May 2026 (13 government, 7 private); most were first detected by outside researchers, dark-web monitors or media rather than the institutions.

The Personal Data Protection Act 2026 for the first time requires notification of the relevant authority when a data breach occurs; TGI says broad exemptions for state agencies, delayed implementation and weak accountability remain concerns.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Research body whose report documents 68 data breaches 2023 to May 2026, including attempted intrusions into the migrant workers' database

headline_en: Start of change in 180 days: new initiatives in economy, diplomacy and welfare (opinion by PM's deputy press secretary)
summary_en: An opinion piece by Shahadat Swadhin, the Prime Minister's deputy press secretary, lists the Tarique Rahman government's six-month initiatives. For migrants, it says a special 'Probashi card' was to start on a pilot basis from August 2026, projects are being taken up for training and language learning for outbound citizens, talks are under way with several countries on setting up training centres in Bangladesh, and the PM's Malaysia visit helped labour market expansion.

facts.statement: The PM's deputy press secretary writes that a special 'Probashi card' (প্রবাসী কার্ড), aimed at improving expatriates' social status, legal protection and living standards and planned under PM Tarique Rahman's direct direction, was going to be launched on a pilot basis from August 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Shahadat Swadhin, PM's deputy press secretary (opinion)

facts.statement: The writer says projects are being taken up to ensure training and language learning for citizens going abroad, and that meaningful discussions are under way with several countries on setting up training centres in Bangladesh.
The writer says the Prime Minister's visit to Malaysia helped labour market expansion, foreign investment and trade, and that talks on a Bangladesh-Malaysia free trade agreement (FTA) have begun.
The writer says the government approved a budget for building new technical schools and colleges nationwide, giving special priority to technical education.

headline_en: 'What use is a house now, when my two boys are gone?' (families of Saudi fire victims left with migration debts)
summary_en: Families in Naogaon of Bangladeshis killed in the 9 August 2026 fire at a sofa factory in Manfuha, Riyadh (16 Bangladeshis dead, 13 from Naogaon) are left with large debts taken to send the workers abroad. Moyna Begum lost two sons whose migration loans now total 8 lakh taka with interest; Rubel Pramanik had gone three months earlier on borrowed money; Shahinur Rahman took a 5.7 lakh taka loan from a samity against his homestead land five months earlier, and his widow fears the samity may take the land.

facts.statement: On Sunday 9 Aug 2026 around 12 noon local time, a fire at a sofa-making factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, killed 16 Bangladeshis, 13 of them from Naogaon, including four from Gondogoali village, Atrai upazila alone.

Mohon Pramanik (22) of Gondogoali, Atrai, Naogaon went to Saudi Arabia seven years before his death by mortgaging land and taking a loan of 4 lakh taka from a samity (savings association); with interest the debt has grown to 8 lakh taka, still unpaid when he died in the 9 Aug 2026 Riyadh fire.

Shahinur Rahman of Registripara, Par-Naogaon, Naogaon municipality went to Saudi Arabia about five months before Aug 2026 after taking a loan of 5 lakh 70 thousand taka from a samity, mortgaging homestead land at Par-Boalia, Naogaon Sadar; he was killed in the Riyadh fire before repaying, and his widow fears the samity people may take the homestead land if the loan is not repaid.

Rubel Pramanik of Atrai, Naogaon was sent to Saudi Arabia about three months before Aug 2026 with borrowed money (amount not stated) to repay family debts; he was killed in the 9 Aug 2026 Riyadh factory fire, leaving a daughter born 16 days earlier.
Families of the Riyadh fire victims in Naogaon say that besides waiting for the bodies, their biggest problem is repaying loans taken for the migration and supporting the household.
